title.full: Global energy and climate outlook 2024 – Updating NDCs and closing the ambition gap – Indicators for 1.5°C alignment

description: Global model extrapolating trends under currently legislated policies.
pathwayDescription: The European Commission’s Global Energy and Climate Outlook 2024 (GECO) provides an ensemble of energy transition scenarios, developed by the Joint Research Centre. Its Reference scenario reflects a continuation of currently legislated and implemented policies only, without incorporating aspirational pledges or long-term strategies. Under this scenario, global CO₂ emissions remain relatively flat in the medium term, with only limited reductions after peaking in the 2020s. The Reference pathway leads to a global temperature increase of approximately 2.6 °C by 2100, significantly above the Paris Agreement goals.

coreDrivers.policies: The pathway is aligned with current and legislated policies: the pathway includes policies legislated as of June 2024 with no additional pledged targets.
coreDrivers.emissionsTargets: Legislated policies drive emissions forecast; resulting a pathway with a 2.6°C end-century warming.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: Technology learning rates are endogenously developed in the model, based on learning curve literature. The overall technology cost trend decreases based on the adoption of individual technologies and their unit costs.
coreDrivers.investmentChange: Annual power-sector investment increases by 40% through 2050, with wind and solar accounting for around two-thirds of total investment, while fossil-fuel power investment remains material. However, GDP doubles over the same period, meaning that power-sector investment declines as a share of GDP.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: Population and GDP assumptions are shared across the GECO scenarios and set the activity baseline. Inputs combine World Bank, IMF, OECD/SSP2, EU Ageing Report, and JRC-IIASA sources.

dependencies.dependency_description: Legislated power policies drive the mix with exogenous capacity additions and technology mix inputs, but they do not require full decarbonisation and the fossil fuels remain in the energy mix.
Renewables penetration is lower in this scenario, as fossil fuel power plants remains active. This means lower demand on grid flexibility and transmission capacity.
Renewable-power employment grows in the Reference pathway, implying some workforce expansion, but GECO does not identify shortages, skills bottlenecks or higher unemployment.
